heading_path: Legal Basis for the Publication of the Budget Review and Outlook Paper

blocks.text: The Budget Review and Outlook Paper is prepared in accordance with Section 26 of the Public Finance Management Act, 2012.  The law states that:
heading_path: Legal Basis for the Publication of the Budget Review and Outlook Paper

blocks.text: The National Treasury shall prepare and submit to -Cabinet for approval, by the 30 th  September in each financial year, a Budget Review and Outlook Paper, which shall include:
heading_path: Legal Basis for the Publication of the Budget Review and Outlook Paper

blocks.text: Actual fiscal performance in the previous financial year compared to the budget appropriation for that year;
heading_path: Legal Basis for the Publication of the Budget Review and Outlook Paper

blocks.text: Updated macro-economic and financial forecasts with sufficient information to show changes from the forecasts in the most recent Budget Policy Statement
heading_path: Legal Basis for the Publication of the Budget Review and Outlook Paper

blocks.text: Information on how actual financial performance for the previous financial year may have affected compliance with the fiscal responsibility principles or the financial objectives in the latest Budget Policy Statement; and
heading_path: Legal Basis for the Publication of the Budget Review and Outlook Paper

blocks.text: The reasons for any deviation from the financial objectives together with proposals to address the deviation and the time estimated to do so.
heading_path: Legal Basis for the Publication of the Budget Review and Outlook Paper

blocks.text: Cabinet shall consider the Budget Review and Outlook Paper with a view to approving it, with or without amendments, not later than fourteen days after its submission.
heading_path: Legal Basis for the Publication of the Budget Review and Outlook Paper

blocks.text: Not later than seven days after the BROP has been approved by Cabinet, the National Treasury shall:
heading_path: Legal Basis for the Publication of the Budget Review and Outlook Paper

blocks.text: Submit the paper to the Budget Committee of the National Assembly to be laid before each house of Parliament; and
heading_path: Legal Basis for the Publication of the Budget Review and Outlook Paper

blocks.text: Publish and publicize the paper not later than fifteen days after laying the Paper before Parliament.

blocks.text: Executive Summary

This Budget Review and Outlook Paper (BROP), is prepared in accordance with the Public Finance Management (PFM) Act, 2012 and its regulations. It presents a review of the budget performance  for  the  FY  2016/17  and  how  the  budget  adhered  to  the  fiscal  responsibility principles and financial objectives sets out in the PFM Act, 2012. It further provides updated macro-economic and financial forecasts with sufficient information to show changes from the projections outlined in the 2017 Budget Policy Statement (BPS) and sets out the broad fiscal parameters for the FY 2018/19 budget and the medium term.

Preliminary fiscal outcome for the FY 2016/17 indicate that the cumulative revenue collection including A-i-A was Ksh 1,400.6 billion. This revenue was Ksh 54.8 billion below the revised target of Ksh 1,455.4 billion due to shortfall in ordinary revenue collection (by Ksh 5.5 billion) following reduced collections from excise duty and corporate income tax; and the shortfall in the collection of cumulative ministerial A-i-A (by Ksh 49.2 billion). The total expenditure and net  lending  amounted  to  Ksh  2,110.0  billion,  against  a  target  of  Ksh  2,327.0  billion.  The shortfall of Ksh 217.0 billion was attributed to lower absorption recorded in both recurrent (Ksh 58.8 billion) and development expenditures by the National Government (Ksh 158.1 billion).

The fiscal deficit for the FY 2016/17, (on a commitment basis and excluding grants), was at Ksh 709.4 billion (equivalent to 9.2 percent of GDP) against a projected deficit of Ksh 871.6 billion (equivalent to 11.7 percent of GDP). Including grants, the fiscal deficit was 8.9 percent of GDP compared with a projected deficit of 10.9 percent of GDP.

The  fiscal  outcome  for  the  FY  2016/17  budget  was  satisfactory  and  adhered  to  the  fiscal responsibility principles and financial objectives set out in the PFM Act, 2012. The National Government development expenditure as a percent of total budget was 35.4 percent well above the  benchmark  of  30.0  percent;  the  share  of  National  Government  wages  and  benefits  to National Government revenues was 30.2 percent, well below the target of 35.0 percent and the National Government net domestic borrowing amounted Ksh 309.8 billion compared to Ksh 357.8  billion  spending  on  domestically  funded  capital  expenditures,  an  indication  that borrowing  financed  only  development  expenditures.  Public  debt  and  obligations  were maintained at a sustainable level and fiscal risks were managed prudently. The reforms in the tax  administration  and  legislations  were  carried  out  to  lock  in  predictability  and  enhance compliance with the tax system.

The Kenyan economy, has continued to experience challenges in 2017, particularly the negative impact  of  the  severe  drought  that  started  in  2016,  the  prolonged  electioneering  period  that culminated in the August 2017 General elections and the repeat of the Presidential Election slated for October 2017, as well as the subdued credit growth to the private sector that have combined to weaken growth and created additional expenditure pressures.

In light of emerging expenditure pressures, we have reviewed the FY 2017/18 budget in the context  of  Supplementary  I,  which  was  recently  submitted  to  the  National  Assembly  for approval. In the estimates, the additional expenditures have been accommodated by tradeoffs and reallocations of the existing budgetary provisions supported by austerity measures instituted on less productive areas of spending across the Government. The less productive budgetary items have been rationalized downwards by between 20 to 75 percent.

In the FY 2018/19, the revenue collection, including Appropriation-in-Aid (AiA) is projected to  increase  to  18.8  percent  of  GDP  from  18.7  percent  of  GDP  in  FY  2017/18.  Overall expenditure and net lending is projected at 25.2 percent of GDP, down from the projected 26.8 percent of GDP in the FY 2017/18.

The fiscal balance excluding grants, is therefore projected at 6.4 percent of GDP in the FY 2018/19.  Including  grants,  the  overall  fiscal  balance  is  projected  at  5.9  percent  of  GDP compared  to  the  estimated  overall  fiscal  balance  of  7.4  percent  of  GDP  in  FY  2017/18. Excluding expenditures related to the SGR, the deficit in the FY 2018/19 is projected at 5.4 percent of GDP, down from 6.8 percent of GDP in FY 2017/18.The fiscal deficit in FY 2018/19, will be financed by net external financing of 2.1 percent of GDP and net domestic financing of 3.8 percent of GDP.

This  macroeconomic  outlook  is  not  without  risks.  The  uncertainties  in  the  global  markets occasioned by the U.S. economic policies, the post-Brexit resolution, the pace of normalization of  monetary  policies  in  advanced  economies  and  the  recent  geopolitical  tensions  building around production and use of nuclear weapons are likely to weigh down global growth with negative impact on trade and financial flows.

Additionally,  the  economy  continues  to  be  exposed  to  adverse  weather  conditions  in  the medium term. Further, there are salary and recurrent expenditure pressures that continue to create fiscal risks. The Government will closely monitor these risks and undertake appropriate measures to safeguard macroeconomic stability should these risks materialize.
I. INTRODUCTION
Objective of the 2017 Budget Review and Outlook Paper
heading_path: Objective of the 2017 Budget Review and Outlook Paper

blocks.text: 1. The objective of the 2017 Budget Review and Outlook Paper (BROP) is to provide a review of fiscal performance for the FY 2016/17 and how this performance impacts on the financial  objectives  and  fiscal  responsibility  principles  set  out  in  the  2017  Budget  Policy Statement  (BPS).  The  document  provides  highlights  of  recent  economic  developments  and outlook and sector ceilings for the FY 2018/19 budget and the medium term.
heading_path: Objective of the 2017 Budget Review and Outlook Paper

blocks.text: 2. The sector ceilings are guided by the overall resource envelope that is informed by the macroeconomic and fiscal outlook as presented in section III and IV of this document. The sector ceilings set in motion the budget preparation for the FY 2018/19 and the medium term.
heading_path: Objective of the 2017 Budget Review and Outlook Paper

blocks.text: 3. As required by the PFM Act, 2012, budget process aims to promote the efficient and effective use of resources, based on evidence and rational deliberation. To achieve this, the Government remains committed to a measured, prudent course of fiscal consolidation to narrow the budget deficit and stabilize debt.
heading_path: Objective of the 2017 Budget Review and Outlook Paper

blocks.text: 4. In this  context,  the  2017  Budget  Policy  Statement  (BPS)  set  out  a  series  of macroeconomic policies, proposals to raise additional revenue and sustain core expenditure, improve value for money spent, stabilise the public finances, and contribute to economic growth and  employment  creation.  As  a  result  of  the  improved  fiscal  discipline  and  competent management of the economy, the macro-indicators for the FY 2017/18 are pointing in the right direction. The economy continues to register robust growth while macroeconomic stability is preserved.
heading_path: Objective of the 2017 Budget Review and Outlook Paper

blocks.text: 5. To meet the current commitments as contained in the 2017/18 Budget, the Government proposed tax measures aimed at raising the tax revenue and providing incentives for industries to thrive and create employment opportunities.
heading_path: Objective of the 2017 Budget Review and Outlook Paper

blocks.text: 6. However, the underperformance in both revenue collection and expenditure in the FY 2016/17 has implications on the financial objectives outlined in the 2017 BPS and the 2017/18 Budget. In particular, the baseline for projecting both the revenue and expenditures for the FY 2017/18 and the medium term has changed given the end FY 2016/17 and quarter one FY 2017/18 as well as the implications of the recent supplementary budget.
heading_path: Objective of the 2017 Budget Review and Outlook Paper

blocks.text: 7. To remedy these deviations, the 2017 BROP details appropriate revisions taking into account the budget outturn for the FY 2016/17. In addition, the fiscal outlook contained in this BROP focuses on reforming the tax and revenue administration systems to enhance revenue yields, promote compliance and facilitate private sector growth and development as indicated in the 2017 BPS.  Further, the National Treasury has issued guidelines on how capital projects should be planned, appraised and evaluated before funds are committed in the budget.
heading_path: Objective of the 2017 Budget Review and Outlook Paper

blocks.text: 8. With this background, the rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section II provides a  review of the fiscal performance for the FY 2016/17 and its implications on the financial objectives set out in the 2017 BPS. This is followed by Section III that provides highlights of the recent economic developments and outlook. The proposed Resource Allocation Framework is provided in Section IV while conclusion is in Section V.

blocks.text: II. REVIEW OF FISCAL PERFORMANCE FOR THE FY 2016/17
heading_path: II. REVIEW OF FISCAL PERFORMANCE FOR THE FY 2016/17

blocks.text: A. Overview

9. The  implementation  of  the  budget  for  FY  2016/17  progressed  well  and  picked  up towards the end of the fiscal year. However, both revenue collection and expenditures lagged behind their respective targets. Total revenues was Ksh 1,400.6 billion indicating a Ksh 54.8 billion  shortfall  against  the  revised  target  of  Ksh  1,455.4  billion  This  reflects  shortfalls  in Appropriation in Aid (Ksh.49.2 billion), excise duty (Ksh.4.8 billion) and Import Declaration Fees (Ksh.1.7 billion), Other income tax including Corporate Income Tax (Ksh.17.4 billion) while  Pay  as  You  Earn  (PAYE)  recorded  an  over  performance  giving  a  marginal  over performance of Ksh.1.2 billion in the total income tax. Therefore the ordinary revenues were broadly on target with a slight shortfall of Ksh.5.5 billion. Appropriation in aid shortfall of Ksh.49.2 billion is in part explained by delayed reporting by the collecting MDAs, we expect this shortfall to narrow when the MDAs present their final accounts statements.

Total expenditures was Ksh 2,110.0 billion against the revised target of Ksh 2,326.9 billion, falling short of the revised target by 216.9 billion. The shortfall was occasioned by the lower absorption of both recurrent and development expenditures by the National Government. In particular, lower absorptions were recorded in both the recurrent (wages and salaries and operations and maintenance) and development expenditures by the National Government. Total expenditures and net lending by end of June 2017.

As  a  result,  the  fiscal  balance  as  at  end  of  June  2017  (on  a  commitment  basis  and excluding grants) was Ksh 709.4 billion (equivalent to 9.2 percent of GDP) against a projected deficit of Ksh 871.6 billion (equivalent to 11.7 percent of GDP). Inclusive of grants, the fiscal deficit was 8.9 percent of GDP compared with the projected deficit of 10.9 percent of GDP. Excluding expenditures related to standard Gauge Railway, the deficit was 7.4 percent of GDP in FY 2016/17.

The  fiscal  outcome  for  the  FY  2016/17  budget  adhered  to  the  fiscal  responsibility principles and financial objectives set out in the PFM Act, 2012.  The National Government development  expenditure  as  a  percent  of  total  budget  was  35.4  percent  well  above  the benchmark of 30.0 percent; the share of National Government wages and benefits to National Government revenues was 30.2 percent, well below the target of 35.0 percent and the National Government net domestic borrowing amounted Ksh 309.8 billion compared to Ksh 357.8 billion spending on domestically funded capital expenditures, an indication that borrowing financed only development expenditures. Public debt and obligations were maintained at a sustainable level  and  fiscal  risks  were  managed  prudently.  The  reforms  in  the  tax  administration  and legislations  were  carried  out  to  lock  in  predictability  and  enhance  compliance  with  the  tax system.

Expenditure Performance

The under-spending was in respect of operations and maintenance (Ksh 80.5 billion), wages and salaries (Ksh 4.5 billion), as well as pensions and other contribution funds (Ksh 1.3 billion). Expenditure on domestic interest payments was above the target by Ksh 31.1 billion while foreign interest was below target by Ksh 4.0 billion. blocks.text: D. Fiscal Responsibility Principles
33. In line with the Constitution, the Public Finance Management (PFM) Act, 2012, the PFM regulations, and in keeping with prudent and transparent management of public resources,
the Government has adhered to the fiscal responsibility principles as set out in the statute as follows:

The National Government's development expenditure as a percent of total budget was 35.4 percent in FY 2016/17 and is set to remain above the 30 percent minimum threshold set out in the PFM law over the medium term (Table 5).

The law requires that the national government's expenditure on the compensation of employees  (including  benefits  and  allowances)  shall  not  exceed  35  percent  of  the  national government's equitable share of the revenue raised nationally plus other revenues generated by the national government pursuant to Article 209 (4) of the Constitution. In conformity to this regulation, the National Government share of wages and benefits to revenues was 30.2 percent in the FY 2016/17, and is projected at 31.5 percent in the FY 2017/18, declining to 24.9 percent by FY 2020/21.

The fiscal principle of ensuring the national government's borrowing is used only for financing  development  expenditures  continues  to  be  adhered  to.  The  Medium  Term  Debt Strategy and other policy documents spells out the purposes of external and domestic financing. The resources mobilized through borrowing during the fiscal year 2016/17 were strictly used to finance infrastructure projects as defined in the development estimates of the budget.
The Government is required to maintain public debt at a sustainable level as approved by Parliament (for National Government) and County Assemblies (for County Governments)

38. The baseline public debt path remains consistent with the EAC convergence criteria (deficit and debt) and below the relevant public debt benchmark. The public debt sustainability indicators illustrates that Kenya continues to face  a low risk of debt distress as it remains below the threshold of 74 percent of GDP in net present terms. In 2017 the PV of debt is estimated at 49.0 percent of GDP and projected to decline to 43.2 percent of GDP by 2021. The PV of public sector debt to revenue ratio is similarly within its threshold of 300 percent. In 2017, the PV of public sector debt to revenue ratio is estimated at 235.7 percent and is projected to improve to 201.4 percent by 2021. This debt performance is attributed to the high level of concessionality of current external debt and a positive outlook in macroeconomic indicators.

39. To  manage  fiscal  risks  prudently  as  required,  the  Government  has  improved  its macroeconomic forecasts and regularly reviews the impact of macroeconomic projections and their  implications  on  the  budget. In order to lock in predictability and enhance compliance with tax system, the government through the Finance Act, 2016, amended the income Tax Act, Excise Duty Act, VAT Act and the Tax Procedure Act. 42. The broad development policies of the Government provide a clear and progressive approach to stimulate inclusive growth. Implementation  of  the  priority programs  will  be  monitored  closely  so  as  to  realize  benefits  and  maintain  positive  growth momentum, create jobs, reduce poverty and inequality. Some of the programs include:
 Create 1.3 million jobs every year and work with county governments to establish at least one industry in every county.
 Establish a government sponsored apprenticeship programme of up to 12 months for all university and TVET graduates.
 Double the number of vulnerable citizens supported through the cash transfer programme (Inua Jamii) from 700,000 to 1,400,000. This will include all citizens above the age of 70;

 Facilitate mass housing production of at least 500,000 affordable homes in 5 years across the  country  by  working  in  partnership  with  financial  institutions,  private  developers, manufacturers of building materials and cooperatives to deliver homes faster and reduce the cost of construction by at least 50%.
 Expand free maternity care to include government funded NHIF cover for every expectant mother for one year.
 Ensure every citizen is connected to reliable and affordable electricity (on or off-grid) by 2020.

 Expand food and agricultural production, double the fertiliser subsidy initiative, reducing the cost to farmers to less than Ksh1,500. Expand the programme to include all crops with a resultant increase in production and support the expansion and capacity of local fertiliser manufacture.

 Complete the 57-large-scale dam construction programme, support small-holder agricultural  irrigation  and  work  with  the  private sector  to  enhance food  and agricultural production on at least 1.2 million acres.

 Make  government  more  transparent  and  accountable  through  the  digitisation  of  all government procurement; expand and deliver e-government services through the growing network of Huduma Centres.

blocks.text: 53. An increasing number of County Governments are unable to stay within the wage bill threshold of 35 percent of total revenue as defined in section 25(1) (a,b) of the PFM (County Governments) Regulations. In the FY 2013/14, 19 Counties were unable to stay within this limit. This number increased to 29 in the FY 2014/15 and 30 in the FY 2015/16. Preliminary data  for  the  first  nine  months  of  FY  2016/17  shows  that  26  Counties  were  noncompliant, although this number could change depending on OSR performance and personnel emoluments during the last quarter. The non-compliance with the wage bill limit set in the PFM Act by Counties is primarily due to the following factors:

blocks.text:  Violation  of  Salaries  and  Remuneration  Commission  (SRC)  guidelines  on  job  grading, salary structures and compensation of employees including payment of sitting allowances as well as regulations on use of approved staff establishments, and payment of staff through the Integrated Payroll and Personnel Database (IPPD).
heading_path: F. County Governments' Compliance with the PFM Act

blocks.text:  High fixed costs inherited by some Counties relative to their equitable share transfer. The costs -- predominantly salaries of national civil servants performing devolved functions and former Local Authority staff -- are not factored in the criteria for horizontal distribution of revenue. To assist these fiscally-constrained Counties, the National Government will pursue implementation of recommendations contained in the Capacity Assessment and Rationalization of the Public Service (CARPS) report.
heading_path: F. County Governments' Compliance with the PFM Act

blocks.text:  Challenges encountered in OSR collection leading to less than optimal revenue yield vis-àvis potential.
heading_path: F. County Governments' Compliance with the PFM Act

blocks.text: 54. Analysis  of  the  County  Governments  audited  accounts  has  identified  additional noncompliance issues relating to the PFM Act as follows:
heading_path: F. County Governments' Compliance with the PFM Act

blocks.text:  Weak  internal  controls  and  absence  of  audit  committees :  Some  Counties  have  not established internal audit committees as required in section 155 of the PFM Act. Where the committees exist, they lack necessary autonomy. Internal audit committees are expected to review governance mechanisms and undertake audits with the objective of strengthening internal controls.
heading_path: F. County Governments' Compliance with the PFM Act

blocks.text:  Procurement irregularities :  The  Auditor-General  has  cited  numerous  violations  of  the Public  Procurement  and  Asset  Disposal  Act,  2003.  The  violations  include:  variation  of contract sums and inflation of contract prices; unsupported and unexplained payments, or full payment for incomplete, abandoned and stalled projects; unconfirmed asset purchases due to poor maintenance of fixed asset registers; and unjustified single sourcing of supplies, service  providers and contractors.  In  their approved  budgets,  the  Counties  are failing  to disclose costs of projects rolled over from previous financial years. In addition, funds are reallocated to different projects without approval procedures contained in section 154 of the PFM Act.
heading_path: F. County Governments' Compliance with the PFM Act

blocks.text:  Accumulation of pending bills and arrears : All the Counties have accumulated pending bills attributed to nonpayment of contractors and suppliers of goods and services, and of salaries. Some Counties have also failed to remit statutory deductions (including employee pension contributions) to respective institutions.
heading_path: F. County Governments' Compliance with the PFM Act

blocks.text:  Financial statements unreconciled with balances in the Integrated Financial Management Information System (IFMIS): A number of Counties do not post all their
heading_path: F. County Governments' Compliance with the PFM Act

blocks.text: transactions -- receipts from the Exchequer and OSR as well as payments -- on IFMIS. As a result, budget execution as captured in annual financial statements differs from balances in the system.
heading_path: F. County Governments' Compliance with the PFM Act

blocks.text:  Poor management of County mortgage and car loan funds: In many Counties, funds were  directly  transferred  to  beneficiaries,  who  did  not  deposit  securities  with  the  fund managers. Loan and mortgage repayment was pegged on beneficiaries' allowances rather than their salaries. A number of funds are uninsured, exposing them to contingent liabilities in the event of defaults or upon expiry of beneficiaries' employment contracts. Section 116 of the PFM Act requires the County Executive Committe Member for Finance to appoint an  administrator  for  each  fund.  The  administrator  is  required  to  ensure  that  loans  are recovered via the IPPD system, keep custody of all collateral and submit quarterly financial statements to the County Treasury with a copy to the Controller of Budget in line with section 168(3) of the PFM Act.
heading_path: F. County Governments' Compliance with the PFM Act

blocks.text:  Failure to establish County Budget and Economic Forums: Section 137 of the PFM Act requires Counties to establish, operationalize Budget and Economic Forums as a means of consultation  during  preparation  of  budgets  as  well  as  plans,  Fiscal  Strategy  Papers  and Budget Review and Outlook Papers. A number of Counties have not yet established these forums.

heading_path: III. RECENT ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENTS AND OUTLOOK

blocks.text: A. Overview

56. On the domestic scene, the Kenyan economy has continued to experience challenges in 2017.  The  negative  impact  of  the  severe  drought  that  started  in  2016,  the  prolonged electioneering period that culminated in the August 2017 General elections and the repeat of the Presidential Election slated for October 2017, as well as the subdued credit growth to the private  sector  have  combined  to  weaken  growth.  These  developments  have  resulted  in uncertainties among investors, business community and consumers as they adopt a wait and see attitude, thus weighing down the growth outlook.

57. Given the above developments the growth outlook for 2017 has been revised down to 5.1 percent from 5.5 percent as earlier projected and 5.9 percent in the 2017 Budget Policy Statement (BPS). This notwithstanding, the economy has remained resilient recording a growth of 5.0 percent in Quarter 2 of 2017, up from 4.7 percent in Quarter 1. This growth momentum reflects the continued impact of the public infrastructural investment across the country and the resilient  domestic  demand  as  well  as  the  stable  macroeconomic  environment.  Indeed,  the Standard and Poor's in their release in September 2017, affirmed Kenya's short and long term foreign  and  local  currency  sovereign  credit  rating  at  B+/B  citing  Kenya's  strong  growth prospects which will facilitate fiscal consolidation.

58. Overall month on month inflation declined to 7.1 percent in September 2017 (within Government target range of 5+/-2.5 percent) from 8.0 percent in August 2017. The decline was due to fall in the cost of some food items which was mainly attributed to a relief from a situation of depressed supply of goods and services as experienced in August 2017. In the twelve month to September 2017, the average annual inflation rate was 8.4 percent compared to 6.5 percent in  the same period in 2016. Inflation is expected to decline and fall within the Government target range of 5+/-2.5 percent in the current fiscal year.

59. The foreign exchange market has remained stable supported by relatively lower import bill, improved tea and horticulture export earnings, strong remittance inflows and a recovery of tourism receipts. On the balance, these developments and strong capital inflows resulted in a narrower current account balance of 5.8 percent of GDP in July 2017 from 6.3 percent in June 2017.  This  has  led  to  a  stable  Kenya  shilling  exchange  rate.  The  official  foreign  exchange reserves increased to US$ 8.1 billion (5.4 months of import cover) as at July 2017, compared to US$ 7.5 billion (4.9 months of import cover) at end of January 2017.
B. Recent Developments
Real Sector Developments

60. The economy grew by 5.8 percent in 2016 compared to 5.7 percent growth in 2015. Growth, remained fairly resilient in the first and second quarter of 2017, recording 4.7 percent and 5.0 percent, respectively despite sharp increases in food prices as a result of adverse weather conditions and a notable rise in international oil prices. This strong growth in the second quarter of 2017 was supported by robust activities in accommodation and restaurant (13.4 percent); real estate (9.7 percent); information and communication (9.2 percent); transport and storage (8.2 percent); construction (7.5 percent) and wholesale and retail trade (2.8 percent). On the other hand, the growth was somewhat constrained by subdued performances in agriculture forestry and fishing, manufacturing, electricity and financial intermediation sectors. (Chart 1 and Table 9).

Growth in the sector was further buoyed by the introduction of passenger rail transport services using the SGR between Mombasa and Nairobi in the month of June. Money Supply

71. Growth of broad money supply, M3, improved to 8.3 percent in the year to July 2017 compared to a growth of 6.9 percent in the year to July 2016. The improved growth in the year to July 2017 was largely on account of an improvement in the uptake of domestic credit and growth of net foreign assets (NFA) of the Central Bank.
Private Sector Credit

72. Annual growth of credit to the private sector recorded a slight increase to 1.6 percent over the 12 months to August 2017 from 1.4 percent in July 2017, reversing the downward trend witnessed since August 2015. The real estate, manufacturing, trade, consumer durables and private households have continued on a net basis to receive credit flows from the banking sector since January 2017.
External Sector Developments

73. The overall balance of payments position improved to a deficit of US$ 65.9 million (0.1 percent of GDP) in the year to July 2017 from a deficit of US$ 1,252.9 million (2.0 percent of GDP) in the year to July 2016 (Chart 5). Inflows to the services account increased by 0.3 percent as a result of improvement in the travel services in line with the recovery in tourist arrivals.

75. The flows in the Financial Account increased to US$ 6,541.2 million in July 2017 compared with US$ 3,590.9 million in July 2016. The financial inflows were mainly in the form of direct investment and other investment which stood at US$ 135 million and US$ 7,023 million, respectively in July 2017. C. Medium Term Economic Outlook
Global Growth Outlook

78. Global economy is on a recovery path with the growth expected to pick up to 3.5 percent in 2017 from 3.2 percent in 2016, supported by the recovery of manufacturing and trade, rising investor confidence, favorable global financing conditions, and stabilizing commodity prices.

79. Growth  in  advanced  economies  remains  subdued  reflecting  the  macroeconomic implications of changes in policy assumptions though improving conditions in a number of the euro countries is expected to raise global economic activity. Growth in emerging market and developing economies are projected to see a sustained pick up from 4.3 percent in 2016 to 4.6 percent in 2017 and 4.8 percent in 2018, primarily driven by gradually improving conditions in large  commodity  exporters  that  experienced  recessions  in  2015-16,  caused  by  declining commodity prices.

80. The economic growth in the sub-Saharan African (SSA) region is expected to pick up in 2017 to 2.7 percent from 1.3 percent in 2016 supported by positive growth prospects for South Africa (one of the largest economies in Sub-Saharan Africa), which is experiencing a bumper crop due to better rainfall and an increase in mining output prompted by a moderate rebound in commodity prices. In the East African Community (EAC) region, economic growth is projected to pick up in 2017 supported by ongoing infrastructure investment efforts, strong private consumption and the lower global oil prices.
Domestic Growth Outlook

81. On the domestic scene, the Kenyan economy has continued to experience challenges in 2017 particularly the negative impact of the severe drought that started in 2016, the prolonged electioneering period that culminated in the August 2017 General elections and the repeat of the Presidential Election slated for October 2017, as well as the subdued credit growth to the private  sector  have  combined  to  weaken  growth.  These  developments  have  resulted  in uncertainties among investors, business community and consumers as they adopt a wait and see attitude, thus weighing down the growth outlook.
82. Given the above developments the growth outlook for 2017 has been revised down to 5.1 percent from 5.5 percent as earlier projected and 5.9 percent in the 2017 Budget Policy Statement (BPS).

83. Going forward in terms of fiscal years, the economic growth is projected at 6.5 percent in  the  FY  2018/19  and  7.1  percent  over  the  medium  term  supported  by  improved  global conditions, improved production in agriculture, ongoing recovery of tourism and completion of key public projects in roads, rail and energy generation, resilient exports and benefits from ongoing regional integration efforts. In addition, the strong consumer demand and private sector investment as well as a stable macroeconomic environment in the country will help reinforce this growth.

84. The growth projections over the medium term are aligned to those of the Medium Term Plan  II  (2013-2017)  and  those  in  its  successor  Medium  Term  Plan  III  (2018-2022)  that  are implementing Vision 2030 (Table 10 and Annex Table 1).

Monetary Policy Outlook

Overall month on month inflation remained above target in the first half of 2017 peaking at 11.7 percent in May 2017 mainly due to increased prices of food following the prolonged drought. In subsequent months, inflation declined falling within target in September 2017. This followed reduced prices of food items after weather conditions improved in the second quarter of the year and measures taken by the government to temporary exempt import on maize, sugar and powdered milk.

The continued prudent monetary policy measures coupled with the expected favourable weather outlook and the policy interventions  on food imports will moderate demand-driven inflationary pressures. Further, the stability of the Kenya exchange rate will reinforce the price stability  objective  and  keep  inflation  within  the  Government  target  range  in  the  remainder period of the fiscal year and in the medium term.
The main risks to inflation remain adverse weather that affects agricultural production and their prices, and potential volatility in international oil prices.
The close coordination of fiscal and monetary policies will continue to delivering on price stability and reduction in cost of doing business in the country.
External Sector Outlook

Kenya's international trade is estimated to grow in volume terms with improvements in weather conditions improving earnings from our exports of tea, coffee and horticulture exports. Further,  with  diversification  of  Kenya's  export  products  and  access  to  other  international

markets, Kenya's exports are expected to improve over the medium term. It is also expected that oil prices will remain stable, diaspora remittances resilient and strong receipts from tourism. These developments will support a relatively narrow current account deficit over the medium term and strengthen the Kenya's external position thereby reinforcing stability in the Kenya Shilling exchange rate. In addition, IMF precautionary Arrangement facility of approximately US$ 1,500 million  is  expected  to  provide  additional  buffer  against  short  term  external  and domestic shocks.
Fiscal Policy Outlook

90. Fiscal policy over the medium-term aims at supporting rapid and inclusive economic growth, ensuring a sustainable debt position by narrowing the budget deficit and at the same time supporting the devolved system of Government for effective delivery of services.

91. Over the medium term revenue collection is expected to rise to about 19.4 percent of GDP by FY 2020/21 while expenditures will decline gradually from 26.8 percent of GDP in FY 2017/18 to 24.4 percent of GDP in FY 2020/21. As a result, the overall budget deficit inclusive of grants is projected to decline to 4.6 percent of GDP in the medium term from 8.9 percent in FY 2016/17.
D. Risks to the Domestic Economic Outlook

blocks.text: 92. This  macroeconomic  outlook  is  not  without  risks.  The  uncertainties  in  the  global markets  occasioned  by  the  U.S.  economic  policies,  the  post-Brexit  resolution,  the  pace  of normalization of monetary policies in advanced economies and the recent geopolitical tensions building around production and use of nuclear weapons are likely to weigh down global growth with negative impact on trade and financial flows.

The Kenyan economy in 2017, is experiencing the impacts of a prolonged electoral process that has created uncertainty amongst investors, business community and consumers and has potential adverse impact on tourism and security amongst others, weighing down the growth outlook for 2017.
heading_path: D. Risks to the Domestic Economic Outlook

blocks.text: 94. Additionally, the economy continues to be exposed to adverse weather conditions in the medium term. Further, there are salary and recurrent expenditure pressures that continue to create fiscal risks.

blocks.text: 95. The Government will closely monitor these risks and undertake appropriate measures to safeguard macroeconomic stability should these risks materialize.

blocks.text: IV. RESOURCE ALLOCATION FRAMEWORK
A. Adjustments to the FY 2017/18 Budget
heading_path: A. Adjustments to the FY 2017/18 Budget

blocks.text: 96. As preparations for the FY 2018/19 medium-term budget commence, it is worth noting that the implementation of the FY 2017/18 budget is experiencing challenges particularly on revenue  collection  and  elevated  expenditure  pressures.  The  adverse  spillover  effects  of  the prolonged  drought,  the  repeat  of  Presidential  Election  scheduled  for  October  2017,  salary shortfalls and the under performance of the main revenue tax heads are some of the challenges that have led to the revision of the FY 2017/18 budget.
heading_path: A. Adjustments to the FY 2017/18 Budget

blocks.text: 97. As such the revenue forecasts for FY 2017/18 have been reviewed downwards to reflect outcome  in  FY  2016/17  and  also  taking  into  account  the  fiscal  developments  through  end September 2017. Further, expenditure projections have been revised to accommodate some of these challenges, emerging priorities and provide room for salary shortfalls under the recently approved supplementary budget I. These additional expenditures have been accommodated by tradeoffs and reallocations of the existing budgetary provisions supported by austerity measures instituted  on  less  productive  areas  of  spending  across  the  Government.  The  less  productive budgetary items have been rationalized downwards by between 20 to 75 percent in order to accommodate the additional expenditure priorities and to ensure a sustainable fiscal profile that supports economic expansion and sustainable debt position.
heading_path: A. Adjustments to the FY 2017/18 Budget

blocks.text: B. Medium Term Fiscal Projections

98. Over the medium term, driven by continued reforms, revenue collection is expected to rise to about 19.4 percent of GDP by FY 2020/21 (Annex Tables 2 and 3) . Overall expenditures will decline gradually from 26.8 percent of GDP in FY 2017/18 to 24.4 percent of GDP in FY 2020/21. Overall recurrent expenditures are expected to decline from 16.3 percent of GDP in FY  2017/18  to  14.4  percent  in  the  medium  term  while  development  and  net  lending expenditures is projected at 6.9 percent of GDP over the medium term.

99. The overall budget deficit inclusive of grants is projected to decline to 4.6 percent of GDP in the medium term, as major infrastructural projects currently being implemented by the Government  are  completed.  This  will  reinforce  policy  of  consistency  and  predictability  of government spending and will be achieved through the following strategies:
 Directing more resources coming from enhanced revenue collection to development related activities as we curtail recurrent spending;
 Ensuring efficient and effective public spending; and
 Ensuring that capital expenditure proposals have been thoroughly scrutinized  and prioritized so that only high impact projects are accommodated using scarce resources.
C. FY 2018/19 Budget Framework

100. The  FY  2018/19  budget  framework  is  intended  to  continue  the  fiscal  consolidation agenda with the completion of SGR phase I, shedding off election related expenditures, drought related interventions and other one offs expenditure programmes, particularly those related to security. The overall fiscal deficit including grants is expected to decline from 8.9 percent of GDP in FY 2016/17 to 5.9 percent in FY 2018/19. This consolidation will bolster our debt
sustainability position and give flexibility for counter cyclical fiscal policy interventions when appropriate.

101. Revenue Projections: In the FY 2018/19 revenue collection including Appropriationin-Aid (AiA) is projected to increase to Ksh 1,882.5 billion (18.8 percent of GDP) up from Ksh 1,647.2 billion (18.7 percent of GDP) in the FY 2017/18. This revenue performance will be underpinned by on-going reforms in tax policy and revenue administration. Ordinary revenues will amount to Ksh 1,717.0 billion (17.2 percent of GDP) in FY 2018/19 up from Ksh 1,490.4 billion (16.9 percent of GDP) in FY 2017/18.

102. Expenditure Projections: In the FY 2018/19, overall expenditure and net lending are projected  at  Ksh  2,523.0  billion  (25.2  percent  of  GDP)  up  from  the  estimated  Ksh  2,358.6 billion (26.8 percent of GDP) in the FY 2017/18 revised budget. These expenditures comprises among others, recurrent of Ksh 1,510.2 billion (15.1 percent of GDP), development of Ksh 679.4 billion (6.8 percent of GDP) and other expenditures of Ksh 333.4 billion (3.3 percent of GDP).

103. In terms of percentage of GDP, the wages and salaries bill for teachers and civil servants including the police is expected to reduce to 4.4 percent of GDP in the FY 2018/19 from 4.6 percent in the FY 2017/18. Domestic interest payments are expected to decline to 2.4 percent of GDP in the FY 2018/19 from 2.6 percent of GDP in FY 2017/18.

104. A contingency of Ksh 5.0 billion is provided for in the FY 2018/19 budget. In addition, Ksh 8.6 billion is provided for as conditional grants to marginal areas, an increase from the 7.7 billion provided in the FY 2017/18 budget.

105. Overall deficit and financing: Reflecting the projected expenditures and revenues, the fiscal deficit (excluding grants), is projected at Ksh 640.6 billion (equivalent to 6.4 percent of GDP) in the FY 2018/19. Including grants, the overall fiscal deficit is projected at Ksh 590.1 billion (5.9 percent of GDP) in FY 2018/19 against the estimated overall fiscal balance of Ksh 651.8  billion  (7.4  percent  of  GDP)  in  FY  2017/18.  The  deficit  excluding  SGR  related expenditures in the FY 2018/19 is projected at 5.4 percent of GDP lower than the projected 6.8 percent of GDP in FY 2017/18.

106. The fiscal deficit in FY 2018/19, will be financed by net external financing of Ksh 205.6 billion (2.1 percent of GDP), Ksh 380.3 billion (3.8 percent of GDP) net domestic borrowing and other net domestic receipts of Ksh 4.2 billion.

107. Transfer to County Governments: With Ordinary revenue projections slightly rising from 17.0 percent of GDP in FY 2016/17 to FY 17.2 percent of GDP in the FY 2018/19, and at the same time expenditures under the Consolidated Fund Services (CFS) increasing from 4.8 percent of GDP in FY 2016/17 to 7.5 percent of GDP in FY 2018/19, each level of Government is expected to broadly support the fiscal consolidation. In this respect therefore, the National Government  expenditures  funded  from  domestic  resources  are  projected  to  decline  by  1.5 percent of GDP. Similarly the allocation to County Governments is projected to decline by 0.2 percent of GDP, from 3.5 percent in FY 2017/18 to 3.3 percent in FY 2018/19. The nominal year-on-year growth of allocation to the county governments is projected to remain stable at about 7 percent.
D. Medium-Term Expenditure Framework

108. The  medium-term  priorities  and  strategies  outlined  in  the  Third  Medium-Term  Plan (2018-2022) of the Kenya Vision 2030 will broadly guide the development of sector priorities, policies and plans and subsequent monitoring and evaluation processes for FY2018/19-2020/21 medium-term  Budget.  Resource  allocation  will  continue  to  be  aligned  to  development

programmes/projects under the economic transformation agenda. The fiscal policy stance for the medium-term will be geared towards implementing growth-oriented policies anchored on moderation  of  public  expenditure  growth.  The  composition  of  expenditure  will  focus  on productive capital projects and priority commitments, while protecting budgetary allocations to social  sectors,  namely;  education,  health  and  social  protection.  In  the  FY  2018/19  MTEF Budget,  the Government will pay special attention to the following over the medium-term:
 Programmes focusing on employment creation;
 Establishment of a government sponsored apprenticeship programme for all university and TVET graduates;
 Doubling the number of vulnerable citizens supported through the cash transfer programme (Inua Jamii) and all senior citizens above the age of 70;
 Provision of health insurance cover through the NHIF for all citizens above the age of 70;
 Enhancement of the education programmes to include free day public secondary schools;
 Expanding the free maternity programme to include NHIF cover for postnatal care for one year;
 Increasing connectivity to reliable and affordable electricity (on or off-grid) by 2020;
 Expansion of food and agricultural production and increase the fertilizer subsidy initiative to reduce the cost to farmers;

109. Resources earmarked for strategic interventions in the areas of social welfare, youth empowerment and development of arid regions will be ring-fenced over the medium term. In this regard, we have factored additional resources with a special focus to the following over the medium-term:

 Social Protection, Culture & Recreation - resources to double the number of vulnerable citizens  supported  through  the  cash  transfer  programme  (Inua  Jamii);  and  provision  of health insurance cover through the NHIF for all citizens above the age of 70. Consequently, the allocation to this sector is expected to increase by an overall 20.0 per cent in FY 2018/19 and the medium-term.

 Education -  enhancement of the free primary education programme to include free day public  secondary  schools;  and  establishment  of  a  government  sponsored  apprenticeship programme for all  university  and  TVET  graduates.  Consequently,  the  allocation  to  this sector  is  expected  to  increase  by  an  overall  15.2  per  cent  in  FY  2018/19  and  over  the medium-term.

 Health - expansion of the free maternity programme to include NHIF cover for postnatal care for one year. Consequently, the allocation to this sector is expected to increase by an overall 4.2 per cent in FY 2018/19 and over the medium-term.

 Agriculture,  Rural  &  Urban  Development -  expansion  of  food  and  agricultural production and increase the fertilizer subsidy initiative to reduce the cost to farmers; and support to small-holder agricultural irrigation by constructing large-scale dams. Consequently, the allocation to this sector is expected to increase in FY2018/19 and over the medium-term.

V. CONCLUSION AND NEXT STEPS

111. The  FY  2018/19  and  the  Medium  Term  budget  and  fiscal  framework  projections presented  in  this  BROP  takes  into  account  the  expected  strong  domestic  growth  due  to  the recovery in the global economy, continued public infrastructure investment, enhanced revenue collection following improved  tax  administration as well  as  a  stable  macroeconomic environment.  It  also  takes  into  account  risks  facing  economy  such  as  public  expenditures pressures which may reallocate resources from the productive sectors.

112. As  such,  the  fiscal  strategy  in  this  BROP  will  focus  on  enhancing  overall  revenue collection  and  reallocating  resources  to  productive  sectors  of  the  economy.  The  strategy therefore,  targets  to  maintain  fiscal  discipline  in  all  levels  of  the  government  for  maximum return from public resources in line with the Fiscal Responsibility Principles outlined in the PFM law.

113. Going forward, the set of policies outlined in this BROP ensures continuity in resource allocation  based  on  prioritized  programs  that  have  been  earmarked  by  the  government  to accelerate growth, employment creation and poverty reduction.

114. The policies and sector ceilings in this document will guide the Sector Working Groups and  line  ministries  in  the  preparations  of  the  FY  2018/19  budget  and  is  embedded  on  the priorities  of  the  third  Medium  Term  Plan  (MTP  III)  (covering  2018-2022),  the  successor document of the second MTP (that covered 2013-2017). The ceilings will form inputs into the next Budget Policy Statement (BPS) which will be finalized by mid-February 2018.
